newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-British movie blitz promises controversy.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-British movie blitz promises controversy.

text.p: It's boy meets girl with a difference: Boy A meets Boy B and they become best buddies at school, then years later Boy A meets Girl A and they become lovers. The twist is, Girl A used to be Boy B.
That is the scenario for what is sure to be one of the most controversial films to hit U.S. theatres this year.

"Different for Girls" spearheads the annual invasion of British movies, which in recent years has resulted in multiple Oscars and a host of new stars thanks to a revival of British cinema. But this year is slightly different: Four of the films to cross the pond star the same actor, Rupert Graves, who finds himself in the not-uncomfortable position of engaging in his own personal box office blitz.
The first of his four movies, "Innocent Sleep," opened quietly with no advance publicity this year. While not rocking the cash registers, it is holding its own in art theatres across the country.

But it is "Different for Girls," in which Graves stars with fellow-Brit Steven Mackintosh, that is likely to be the attention grabber. The film explores the problems faced by transsexuals in their struggle to discover and acknowledge their real selves and to find their place in society.
It also delves into society's difficulties in accepting the gender-bending men and women who seek to have their bodies transformed into those of the opposite sex.

Graves plays a 34-year-old macho type locked in the punk era of the '70s who falls in love with his former school pal, now surgically transformed into a woman. Mackintosh, who plays the transsexual, says the film has nothing to apologise for, although he does not expect everyone to accept or like it.

"It is basically a love story, which is a universal theme. It's got the complication of being a love story between a male and a transsexual. That is the subject of the film and it deals with the awkwardness of that," Mackintosh told Reuters.

"It doesn't say that it's a bad thing or a good thing. It acknowledges the difficulty of the subject and I think it's a fair stab at looking at those difficulties and finding a solution to them," he said in an interview.

Is America ready for such a controversial topic? Graves ponders before replying: "I think some of the American audience is ready for it and some of them aren't, probably. You hope as many people see it as can and as many people like it as can. I'm sure some people will like it and some won't."

The film, which will open in New York and Los Angeles on Sept. 12 and go nationwide shortly after, has an all-British cast and was shot in London. But it has a Hollywood twist: director Richard Spence knows a group of transsexual women who meet every month in a bar in the Silverlake area of Los Angeles where their aim, he says, "is not to be noticed, just to be ordinary."

Graves said he and Mackintosh had no difficulty with the sexuality of the film, even when they had to simulate a sex scene. "Actually it was quite funny in a way. Steven had this rubber prosthetic body to give him a woman's shape and it started melting in the heat (of the studio lights). It started to sag a bit. He'd had it on all day and the laws of gravity came into effect."

The film did enlighten him about transsexualism, Graves said. "I didn't give it much thought before, but what I found talking to transsexuals who helped us on the set was their conviction that they were actually in the wrong body before their operation, which I didn't realise before. It's absolutely deep and meaningful to them to make that change."

Graves will also be seen this summer in "Intimate Relations" as a young lodger seduced by a middle-aged, prim- and-proper housewife in a small town in England. The film, based on a true story that ended in tragedy, opens in Los Angeles and New York on Sept. 5 and nationwide on Sept. 19.

Finally, he will be seen opposite Vanessa Redgrave in "Mrs Dalloway," based on Virginia Woolf's 1925 novel. Graves plays a shell-shocked young soldier bearing the emotional scars of First World War battlefields.

A far cry from your typical, classically trained British actor thoroughly schooled in Shakespeare, Graves left school at 15 and joined the circus at 16 as an apprentice clown. After nine months he started doing children's theatre and ended up in London, where he acted on stage.

He was seen by a casting director there and landed his first feature film role in the Merchant Ivory production, "A Room With a View." He has also been seen by American audiences playing non-starring roles in "Where Angels Fear to Tread," "The Madness of King George" and "Damage."
